clauses.clauseText: Responsibility for and authority over all Part 145 operations; primary FAA contact.
Designate AM; provide sufficient qualified personnel; determine noncertificated employees’ abilities.
Sufficient supervisors, appropriately certificated, overseeing personnel unfamiliar with the work.
Familiarity with applicable regulations and inspection methods; proficiency with equipment; article-specific.
Part 65 mechanic/repairman certification; English proficiency.
65.101 eligibility for repairman recommendations; two-year cooling-off for former FAA inspectors.
Management/supervisory, inspection, and RTS rosters; employment summaries; 5-business-day currency.
Initial and recurrent training ensuring capability to perform assigned tasks; 2-year records; revision procedure.
Hazmat-employer training program (49 CFR 171.8/172 Subpart H) and operator-specific hazmat authorization.

clauses.clauseTitle: Need to address safety management and human factors
clauses.clauseText: Why maintenance organisations formally manage safety and human factors, rather than treating them as incidental.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: What industry accident/incident data shows about the role human factors play in maintenance-related events.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: How real maintenance incidents illustrate human factors principles in practice.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: How to recognise conditions or practices with the potential to cause harm before they do.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: How to judge the likelihood and severity of a hazard turning into an actual occurrence.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: How identified risks get reduced to an acceptable level and kept there.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: How an organisation knows whether its risk controls are actually working, not just documented.
clauses.sectionLabel: General/Introduction to Safety Management and Human Factors

clauses.clauseText: Why staff need confidence that honest reporting will be treated fairly, not punitively.
How visible, genuine leadership commitment to safety shapes everyday behaviour on the floor.
How a safety culture adjusts to new risks, technologies, and ways of working over time.
How staff and management stay attentive to safety-relevant conditions rather than becoming complacent.
How individual and group behaviour reflects (and shapes) the organisation's real safety culture.
How safety-relevant information actually flows (or fails to flow) through the organisation.
Established frameworks for understanding why human error happens, as a basis for prevention.

clauses.clauseTitle: Types of errors in maintenance tasks
clauses.clauseText: The recognisable categories of error that occur specifically during maintenance work.
The difference between an honest error and a deliberate departure from procedure, and why that distinction matters.
What a single maintenance error can actually lead to downstream, including for airworthiness.
Practical techniques for reducing error likelihood and catching errors that do occur.
Why humans are not uniformly reliable, and what affects the odds of a task being done correctly.
How the limits of human eyesight affect inspection and detection tasks.
How hearing limitations and workplace noise affect communication and awareness.
How people take in, interpret, and act on information, and where that process can break down.
Why attention is a limited resource, and how perception can be misled.
How people build and lose an accurate picture of what is actually happening around them.
The limits of human memory and why relying on it alone is a known failure point.
How confined-space work and difficult physical access affect performance and safety.
How motivation (or its absence) shapes the quality and care taken in maintenance work.
How general physical and mental fitness for duty affects task performance.
How stress, in useful and harmful amounts, changes how people perform maintenance tasks.
How to recognise and manage workload so it does not overwhelm safe task performance.
How fatigue degrades performance and judgement, often without the person noticing.
How alcohol, medication, and drugs (prescribed or otherwise) impair safe task performance.
How physically demanding maintenance tasks affect fatigue and injury risk.
How doing the same task repeatedly can lead to complacency and missed steps.
How pressure from colleagues can push someone toward an unsafe shortcut.
The range of workplace conditions that add stress on top of the task itself.
How schedule pressure can erode safe practice if not actively managed.
How the volume and pacing of assigned work affects the environment a task is performed in.
How shift patterns, especially night and rotating shifts, affect alertness and performance.
How noise and airborne contaminants in the workplace affect concentration and communication.
How inadequate lighting affects inspection quality and error rates.
How extremes of heat or cold affect physical and mental performance.
How vibration and motion in the work environment affect precision tasks and comfort.
How the complexity of modern aircraft systems raises the stakes of a maintenance error.
Other physical workplace hazards not already covered elsewhere in the syllabus.
How being short-staffed changes workload, pace, and error risk for those on shift.
How interruptions during a task create a well-known, specific error risk (losing your place).
The known limitations of visual inspection as a detection method, and how to compensate for them.
Why accurate, timely recording of work performed matters beyond paperwork compliance.
What happens when written procedure and actual shop-floor practice drift apart, and why that gap is a real risk.
How the availability and quality of technical documentation affects the ability to work safely.

clauses.clauseTitle: Critical maintenance tasks and error-capturing methods
clauses.clauseText: Why certain tasks are treated as critical, and the specific error-capture methods (e.g. independent inspection) used for them.
Why incomplete handover between shifts or individuals is a recurring root cause of maintenance error.
How safety-relevant information reaches (or fails to reach) everyone who needs it.
How differences in language and cultural background can affect communication clarity in a diverse workforce.
How individual and shared responsibility for a task should be understood and assigned.
How effective supervision and leadership support (or undermine) safe task performance.
How decisions get made under real maintenance conditions, individually and as a team.
Why staying current on aircraft type, procedures, and regulation is a personal professional responsibility.
Recognising and avoiding personal habits and shortcuts known to provoke error.
Why speaking up about a safety concern, even to someone more senior, is expected professional behaviour.

clauses.clauseTitle: Safety policy and objectives, just culture principles
clauses.clauseText: The organisation's own stated safety policy, objectives, and its commitment to just culture.

clauses.clauseTitle: Reporting errors and hazards, internal safety reporting scheme
clauses.clauseText: How and why to use the internal safety reporting scheme to report errors and hazards.
How the organisation investigates reported errors, and what staff should expect from that process.
How findings from investigations and reports translate into real corrective action.
How the organisation closes the loop with staff on outcomes, and promotes safety awareness generally.
